paper.title: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate

definition_quote.text: For K > 0, a probabilistic oracle machine M is K-Lipschitz at oracle 𝒪 if, for any other oracle 𝒪′, sup_x |P[M^𝒪(x) = 1] − P[M^𝒪′(x) = 1]| < K · sup_z |P[𝒪(z) = 1] − P[𝒪′(z) = 1]|.
definition_quote.prose: In other words, if M is run with any oracle which assigns similar probabilities to 𝒪, the probability that M outputs 1 should change by at most a K factor more than the maximum difference in the oracle probabilities.

lean_counterpart.summary: Lean uses ≤ instead of <, and compares the oracle with every formal oracle, including itself.
lean_counterpart.code:
/-- An oracle computation is k-Lipschitz if the final probability differs by ≤ k * oracle dist.
    We define this asymmetrically, as we want the neighborhood of a particular oracle. -/
structure Oracle.lipschitz (o : Oracle) (t : ℕ) (k : ℝ) : Prop where
  k0 : 0 ≤ k
  le : ∀ o' : Oracle, |(o.final t).prob true - (o'.final t).prob true| ≤ k * dist o o'

questions.question: Does “any other oracle 𝒪′” include 𝒪 itself?
questions.why: If it does, both sides are zero and the strict < reads 0 < 0, which is false. No machine would then be K-Lipschitz, and Theorem 6.2 would apply to nothing. Lean's ≤ does not have this problem.

questions.question: How are two different oracles at distance zero treated?
questions.why: Two different oracles can give every query the same probability. The right side is then K · 0, so the strict < fails for that pair unless the definition is read as skipping it.

options.label: No such pair exists in the paper's model

questions.question: Which governs: the displayed strict < or the prose “at most”?
questions.why: The prose describes ≤, which matches Lean. If ≤ governs, the strictness part of D01 goes away and only the comparison-domain difference (D02) is left. If < governs, the two questions above decide whether the definition can be met at all.

blocking_rule: If 𝒪′ includes 𝒪 itself and the strict < governs, the paper's definition can never be met, so promotion as stated is refused.

probes.title: Strict versus non-strict bridge
probes.what_it_shows: Lean-checked in the pinned model: a strict bound over every oracle, the oracle itself included, is impossible (0 < 0); a strict bound over different oracles implies Lean's ≤ version; Lean's ≤ version gives a strict bound only with a larger constant and positive distance.

probes.title: Zero-step boundary case
probes.what_it_shows: Lean-checked: with no oracle queries, Lean's ≤ property holds at constant 1, but the strict version over different oracles fails at that constant. The two readings separate even without the self-comparison.

probes.title: Restricted oracle counterexample
probes.what_it_shows: Matching the machine's output law alone does not carry the paper's perturbation bound over to Lean's comparison against every kernel.

probes.title: Oracle representation contract
probes.what_it_shows: A sufficient condition under which a weak (≤) paper-style bound carries over to Lean's universal premise, with a checked example that meets it.

probes.title: Two-query machine
probes.what_it_shows: A small concrete machine where the sufficient condition fails, yet Lean's universal premise still holds at one base: a failed route is not a refutation.

probes.title: Stage-order discriminator
probes.what_it_shows: Letting Bob decide after seeing the coin can change the outcome law, so the claim is limited to a Bob who decides first.

probes.title: Bit-invisible step
probes.what_it_shows: When Bob cannot see the coin, the paper-order step and Lean's step have exactly the same law.

probes.title: Figure 1 round
probes.what_it_shows: One round of the paper's protocol maps to Lean's step only under stated restrictions on Bob and the coin.
